item.title: Genroku Soba: Kurayoshi's Local Noodle Specialty — Guide
item.description: Genroku soba is a beloved local noodle specialty of the Kurayoshi area in central Tottori, a longstanding shop and style that locals return to again and again. Like the wider San’in region, Tottori has its own soba culture, and this is a comforting, everyday bowl rather than a refined delicacy: firm buckwheat noodles in a well-judged broth, served hot or cold with simple toppings. Eating it is the kind of small, authentic pleasure that rounds out a day in the Kurayoshi old town — an unhurried, inexpensive local meal well off the main tourist routes, and a taste of how the region actually eats.

item.title: Kurayoshi White Wall District: Merchant Storehouses on a Canal — Guide
item.description: The white wall district of Kurayoshi, in central Tottori, is a beautifully preserved streetscape of merchant storehouses and townhouses dating from the Edo and Meiji periods. Its signature is the combination of white-plastered walls, dark burnt-cedar boarding and distinctive red iwami-yaki roof tiles, reflected in the water of a small stone-lined canal that runs through the district, crossed by little bridges. Once a prosperous trading town, it has kept its old buildings, which now house craft shops, cafes, sake makers and small museums.

item.title: Tottori Prefectural Museum of Art — Guide
item.description: The Tottori Prefectural Museum of Art is the prefecture’s flagship art museum, a strikingly modern building in Kurayoshi in central Tottori that has quickly become a cultural anchor for the region. Its collection and changing exhibitions span the art of Tottori and the wider San’in region alongside modern and contemporary Japanese and international works, and its architecture — light-filled, open and designed as a public gathering space as much as a gallery — is part of the appeal.

item.title: Tottori Hidden Gems: Secret Beaches, White Walls & Mountain Villages
item.description: Tottori’s fame stops at the sand dunes for most visitors. That’s understandable — they’re extraordinary. But the prefecture’s most lasting impressions often come from somewhere else: a riverside district of white-plastered sake warehouses untouched since the Edo period, a temple wedged impossibly into a cliff cave, a razor-thin strip of sand that separates a lake from the open sea. These places require a little planning and occasionally some nerve, but they offer what crowded attractions cannot — the feeling that you’ve actually found something.
